lessonTitle: The Carnot Cycle: Reversible Limit for Heat Engines

blocks.text: A geothermal plant draws heat from 180 C brine and rejects it to 25 C river water. Whatever the engineers invent, a law of nature caps the fraction of that heat they can turn into work, and the cap can be written down from the two temperatures alone.

blocks.markdown: The **Carnot cycle** is a reversible heat engine cycle that exchanges heat with just two reservoirs, a hot one at $T_H$ and a cold one at $T_L$. Every process is reversible, so there is no friction, no heat transfer across a finite temperature difference and no unrestrained expansion. It is an idealisation, but it sets the upper limit of efficiency for any engine working between the same two temperatures.

items: 1-2: reversible isothermal expansion at $T_H$, heat $Q_H$ absorbed from the hot reservoir.
2-3: reversible adiabatic (isentropic) expansion, temperature falls from $T_H$ to $T_L$.
3-4: reversible isothermal compression at $T_L$, heat $Q_L$ rejected to the cold reservoir.
4-1: reversible adiabatic (isentropic) compression, temperature rises from $T_L$ back to $T_H$.

blocks.markdown: On a **$p$-$V$ diagram** the cycle has two isotherm curves and two steeper adiabat curves enclosing a curved four-sided area equal to the net work. On a **$T$-$s$ diagram** it is a **rectangle**: the isotherms are horizontal lines at $T_H$ and $T_L$ and the isentropes are vertical lines at $s_1$ and $s_2$. The area under the top line is $Q_H=T_H\Delta s$ and under the bottom line is $Q_L=T_L\Delta s$, which is why the efficiency comes out so simply.

blocks.title: Thermal efficiency
blocks.text: Thermal efficiency is the net work output divided by the heat input, $\eta_{th}=W_{net}/Q_H=1-Q_L/Q_H$ (dimensionless). Both heat quantities are taken as positive magnitudes.

blocks.caption: Valid only with absolute temperatures in kelvin
The same four processes in two diagrams; the direction is clockwise on both

blocks.title: Carnot engine between 900 K and 300 K
blocks.prompt: A Carnot engine receives 1500 kJ of heat from a reservoir at 900 K and rejects heat to a reservoir at 300 K. Find the efficiency, the work and the heat rejected.

steps.text: Heat rejected from the energy balance.

blocks.answer: Efficiency 66.7 %, work 1000 kJ, heat rejected 500 kJ.

blocks.markdown: Why can no engine beat the Carnot efficiency? Suppose an irreversible engine did, between the same reservoirs. Run it to drive a reversible Carnot engine backwards as a refrigerator. The combined device would take heat from the cold reservoir and deliver a net amount to the hot one with no net work, a violation of the Clausius statement of the second law. So the assumption is false: **no engine between two reservoirs is more efficient than a reversible one**, and **all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency**, regardless of working fluid.

blocks.title: Steam-plant limit
blocks.prompt: A power plant has boiler steam at 550 C and a condenser at 30 C. What is the maximum possible efficiency? Is a real efficiency of 40 % plausible?

steps.text: The actual efficiency of 40 % is below the limit of 63.2 %, so it is allowed.

blocks.answer: Maximum 63.2 %; 40 % is plausible because it lies below the Carnot value.

blocks.title: Why real engines fall short
blocks.text: Real engines suffer friction, finite temperature differences in heat transfer, throttling and leakage, all irreversibilities. The Carnot value is a ceiling, and raising T_H or lowering T_L is the only way to raise the ceiling.

blocks.title: Using absolute temperatures
blocks.text: Always convert to kelvin before using 1 - T_L/T_H. Using Celsius gives a wrong and sometimes impossible result such as an efficiency of 100 % when T_L = 0 C.

points: The Carnot cycle has two reversible isotherms and two reversible adiabats, and on a T-s diagram it is a rectangle.
Carnot efficiency is 1 - T_L/T_H with absolute temperatures, and it depends on the reservoirs only.
All reversible engines between the same reservoirs have this efficiency; any irreversible one is lower.
No engine can exceed it, because that would violate the second law (Clausius or Kelvin-Planck statement).

questions.stem: A Carnot engine operates between a source at 500 C and a sink at 20 C. Which temperature values must be used in the efficiency formula?

distractorRationale.a: Celsius values give a wrong result.
distractorRationale.c: Converting by simply relabelling units is wrong.
distractorRationale.d: Efficiency depends on the ratio of absolute temperatures.

questions.explanation: The formula 1 - T_L/T_H is derived with the absolute thermodynamic temperature scale. Adding 273.15 to each Celsius value gives 773.15 K and 293.15 K.

questions.stem: On a T-s diagram, the ideal Carnot cycle appears as which shape?

distractorRationale.b: This would be a different cycle.
distractorRationale.d: That would be an isothermal process alone.

questions.explanation: The isothermal processes are horizontal lines at T_H and T_L, and the isentropic processes are vertical lines of constant s. Together they form a rectangle whose area equals the net work.

questions.stem: During which process of the Carnot engine on a p-V diagram is heat absorbed from the hot reservoir?

options.text: The isothermal compression at the lower temperature
The isothermal expansion at the higher temperature

questions.correctOptionText: The isothermal expansion at the higher temperature

distractorRationale.b: That is where heat is rejected.

questions.explanation: Heat is exchanged only during the two isothermal steps, because the adiabats have no heat transfer. Absorbing heat while keeping the temperature at T_H means the gas expands.

questions.stem: An inventor claims a heat engine receiving heat at 500 K and rejecting it at 300 K has an efficiency of 55 %. What should you conclude?

options.text: It is possible if the engine is well designed
It is possible only if the sink is cooled further
It is impossible because efficiencies can never exceed 50 %
It is impossible because the Carnot limit is 40 %

questions.correctOptionText: It is impossible because the Carnot limit is 40 %

distractorRationale.a: No design can beat the reversible limit.
distractorRationale.b: The sink is stated to be at 300 K.
distractorRationale.c: The limit is set by the two temperatures, not 50 %.

questions.explanation: The Carnot efficiency is 1 - 300/500 = 0.40, so no engine between these reservoirs can exceed 40 %. A claim of 55 % violates the second law.

questions.stem: Which argument shows that an irreversible engine cannot be more efficient than a reversible one between the same reservoirs?

options.text: Driving a reversible engine backwards with it would transfer heat from cold to hot with no net work, violating the Clausius statement
A more efficient engine would need less fuel, which is not allowed
Reversible engines have no heat rejection

questions.correctOptionText: Driving a reversible engine backwards with it would transfer heat from cold to hot with no net work, violating the Clausius statement

distractorRationale.b: Fuel use alone is not the argument.

questions.explanation: Take the hypothetical super-efficient engine and use its work to run a reversible engine as a refrigerator between the same reservoirs. The pair would take net heat from the cold body with no work input, which violates the Clausius statement.

questions.stem: A Carnot engine operates between a source at 600 C and a sink at 25 C. Find its efficiency as a percentage (use T(K) = T(C) + 273.15).
questions.explanation: With T_H = 873.15 K and T_L = 298.15 K, the efficiency is 1 - 298.15/873.15 = 0.6585, that is 65.9 %. This is the maximum for any engine between those two reservoirs.

questions.stem: A reversible engine takes 800 kW of heat from gas at 700 K and rejects heat to surroundings at 290 K. What is the maximum power output in kW?
questions.explanation: The efficiency is 1 - 290/700 = 0.5857, so the power is 0.5857 x 800 = 468.6 kW. A real engine would produce less because of irreversibilities.

questions.stem: A designer wants a Carnot efficiency of 60 % with a heat sink at 300 K. What source temperature in kelvin is required?
questions.explanation: Rearranging 0.60 = 1 - 300/T_H gives T_H = 300/(1 - 0.60) = 750 K. This shows how demanding high efficiency is, since it needs a hot source.

questions.stem: Sketch the Carnot heat engine cycle on both p-V and T-s axes. Label the four processes, mark the directions and indicate where heat is absorbed and rejected and what area represents the net work.
markingGuide: Four processes: isothermal expansion at TH, isentropic expansion, isothermal compression at TL, isentropic compression
p-V: two isotherms (shallower) and two adiabats (steeper), clockwise
T-s: rectangle with horizontal isotherms and vertical isentropes, clockwise
Heat absorbed during the high-temperature isotherm, rejected during the low-temperature isotherm
Net work equals the enclosed area on either diagram
questions.explanation: The adiabats are steeper than the isotherms on a p-V diagram, and on T-s the rectangle makes heat the area under each horizontal line. Both diagrams run clockwise for an engine, with the enclosed area equal to the net work.

questions.stem: Explain why no real heat engine operating between two fixed reservoirs can exceed the Carnot efficiency. Name two real irreversibilities that cause real engines to fall short.
markingGuide: Assumes a hypothetical engine with efficiency greater than Carnot between the same reservoirs
Uses its work to drive a reversible Carnot refrigerator between the same reservoirs
Net result: heat moves from cold to hot with no net work, violating Clausius (or the Kelvin-Planck statement)
Therefore no engine can beat the reversible efficiency, and all reversible engines are equal
Examples: friction, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, unrestrained expansion, mixing
questions.explanation: A violation would let heat flow uphill with no work, which the second law forbids. Real irreversibilities such as friction and heat flow across finite temperature differences reduce the efficiency below the reversible value.
